Yeah, well, good question. Is politics on Capitol Hill ever normal, especially these days? You know, we came out of a tumultuous election year into a tumultuous start to the new cycle with the new president, a new Democrat-controlled Congress. The trade-offs are we lose some of our freedom and I think that's a big trade off because I think that's the key ingredient to America's success and prosperity. I think that the debt obviously is going to catch up with us. The chickens will come home to roost at some point. So, you know, whether it's high inflation interest rates through the roof and a terrible sustained recession or a sovereign debt crisis, that's what keeps me up at night long term. The President mentioned infrastructure. I think President Biden's view of infrastructure is much broader than mine. And I don't think we have the trillions of dollars to pay for all this. And I don't think raising taxes is going to help our recovery efforts. I think it's going to drive jobs and capital overseas. We saw the reverse of that when we lowered taxes and regulation. We saw our country and our economy grow. We saw unemployment at record low levels and wages rise. So I obviously have a different view of economic policy. and what drives real and sustained growth. So I am concerned that we would have go back to the highest tax rates in the free world. I do think that in time that might start to bleed into the past through entities like we see mostly in agriculture. The most sinister of the tax hikes will be the death tax and the stepped up basis repealed on the unrealized capital gains. All that to say, because that's very technical speak, I know your producers understand, It means we're going to have to sell the family farm. If this provision passes where the beneficiary of the transfer to state has to pay unrealized capital gains with a stepped up basis being fully repealed and potentially a hike in the debt tax itself or a lower lowering of the exemption, that is a cataclysmic. adverse impact to rural America and to family farmers. They just don't have the cash to pay the taxes. So our new generation young farmers would be in a position where they'd have to liquidate. So I'm fighting hard on that front because I think that's the most urgent and potentially the most disastrous of all that I've heard from President Biden. Broadband infrastructure, I agree, he mentioned rural America once, and he mentioned it in the context of providing the sort of technology backbone to the 35, 40 percent of the rural communities that don't have meaningful access to internet, I agree. I don't want the CCC, which is our Disaster Relief Fund at the Department of Agriculture, to be turned into the carbon bank for the Green New Deal. I think that's, I don't think that's wise. I think we have real disasters like drought, like excessive moisture, like flooding, hurricanes, and like the real threats around the world in terms of trade inequities. I think we have threats to higher taxes, but regardless, CCC has to be preserved. There's not ever enough money to do as much as we'd like to stabilize the ag economy. So that's going to be another. I know I mentioned a lot of things, but you got to have a dashboard of the things that are longer term. And then you've got to have the things in the near term like just getting FSA workers to go back to their jobs since we're all pretty much vaccinated for the most part. I mean, last night's speech, Tim, you had members of Congress and the president and his team fully vaccinated wearing masks and being 50 feet apart. So that tells you something about either the posture of this administration or maybe it's part of the backdrop that they want to continue to propagate so that they can push, you know, and justify a lot of this big government expansion and spending. But at the end of the day, you know, we have to hold the Biden administration accountable for their plans and policies. And I aim to do that every day. I will be relentless about that. But I've never torn anybody down personally that at least in four years that I know of. And I leave that door open to find those small spots where we can say, hey, let's do something good for ag in rural America. Let's do something good for rural health care in hospitals. Let's do something good for ports to planes, get the product, food, fuel, and fiber throughout the nation in a safe and efficient way. I think there's still some things we can do that downside is we're gonna spend too much money and we're gonna drive the debt up to a place that You know, maybe there is a place of no return. I don't know where that is, but we're getting off of close.
